clue.text: Monster from Cyprus left in custody of police

parts.note: CY is the international vehicle code for Cyprus

indicators.note: being in the custody of the police puts the letter inside the word for them

parts.note: cops is an informal word for police

explanation.surface: A creature from Cyprus has been left locked up by the police.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in custody of' locks the L up inside the police, giving CLOPS; CY is the international car code for Cyprus.
explanation.definitionFit: The one-eyed giant of Greek myth is a classic mythical beast.

clue.text: Fantastically hot crowd love traveller in time

indicators.note: fantastically suggests the letters of the two words are arranged in a fanciful new way

parts.note: love is zero in tennis scoring, which looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: A sweaty throng adores a famous figure who journeys through history.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fantastically' rearranges HOTCROWD into DOCTORWH, and O for love finishes it off. Doctor Who is the long-running BBC science-fiction series about a time-travelling alien.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of the BBC series roams through history in a police-box craft, the TARDIS.

clue.text: A cost in dispute about new wintry vehicle

indicators.note: about means the rearranged letters go round the next piece
letters in dispute are at odds and thrown into disorder, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: An argument over the price of a new vehicle for snowy weather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in dispute' turns A COST into SOCAT, and 'about' wraps that round N, giving S-N-OCAT.
explanation.definitionFit: A tracked motor vehicle built for driving over snow and ice.

clue.text: Lazy person before big meal avoiding a hard struggle

indicators.note: before places the first piece ahead of the second in the answer

parts.note: a slug is a slow, idle person

indicators.note: avoiding means the meal word does without the letter a

parts.note: a feast is a large celebratory meal

explanation.surface: An idler, before a banquet, sidesteps a tough fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'avoiding a' takes the A out of FEAST, leaving FEST.
explanation.definitionFit: A slugging match is a bruising, toe-to-toe fight or contest.

clue.text: Guest left on hop? I misconstrued unplanned word

indicators.note: misconstrued suggests the words are wrongly taken, so their letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A visitor leaving on a short jump wonders whether he misread something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'misconstrued' rearranges all fifteen letters of GUEST LEFT ON HOP I.
explanation.definitionFit: An accidental utterance, said without meaning to, is a verbal blunder.

clue.text: University priest, one to celebrate rebellion

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one looks like I
to sing can be to celebrate, as in singing someone's praises

explanation.surface: A college chaplain and someone else get together to celebrate an occasion.
explanation.definitionFit: A rising up against authority is a revolt.

clue.text: Edict of chief at war

indicators.note: of says the answer is taken out of the run of letters that follows

explanation.surface: A decree issued by the commander-in-chief during hostilities.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters sit across 'chieF AT WAr'.
explanation.definitionFit: A ruling on Islamic law issued by a recognised religious authority.

clue.text: Dispatch to punish player

explanation.surface: Sending something away as a way to discipline a sportsperson.
explanation.definitionFit: A farewell or dispatch is a departure; a referee orders a player from the field for a bad foul.

clue.text: Businessman making heap around yard with firm

indicators.note: around means the heap word goes about the other two pieces

parts.note: a ton, or tons, means a large amount, a heap
CO is short for company, a firm

explanation.surface: An entrepreneur builds a pile around his yard with his company.
explanation.definitionFit: A wealthy, powerful industrialist or magnate.

clue.text: Trait in criminal to suppress right? Bothersome factor

indicators.note: to suppress is to hold something down within, so the rearranged letters enclose the next piece
criminal suggests something crooked, so the letters are bent into a new order

explanation.surface: Is a criminal tendency to quash rights a nuisance?
explanation.walkthrough: 'criminal' makes IRITANT, and 'to suppress' holds the R for right down inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that annoys or inflames is an aggravation.

clue.text: Working-class fool upset chap

parts.note: clot is British slang for a fool

indicators.note: upset means the word chap is knocked over and its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: An idiot has upset some fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' rearranges CHAP into HCAP. A cloth cap, the flat cap, is the traditional British symbol of the working man, used as an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: The flat cap was the emblem of the labouring man, so the term labels anything proletarian.

clue.text: Criticism about much of group in race

indicators.note: about means the criticism word goes round the next piece

parts.note: a slam is a harsh criticism

indicators.note: much of means most of the word is used, with its last letter dropped

parts.note: a lot is a group of people or things of one kind, as in 'a bad lot'

explanation.surface: Complaints are made about most of a team taking part in a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'much of' leaves LO, and 'about' wraps the criticism round it. 'race' could suggest ethnicity, but here it is a ski event.
explanation.definitionFit: A downhill ski race weaving between gates is a competition.

clue.text: A fanciful beauty bringing back appropriate drink

parts.note: a peri is a beautiful fairy of Persian legend

indicators.note: bringing back means the next word is turned round

parts.note: fit means suitable or appropriate

explanation.surface: An imaginary lovely brings back a suitable cocktail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bringing back' turns FIT into TIF.
explanation.definitionFit: An alcoholic drink taken before a meal to stimulate the appetite.

clue.text: Fine tree represented island

indicators.note: represented means presented again in another form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A good tree depicted on a Canary island.
explanation.definitionFit: The largest of the Canary Islands, off north-west Africa.

clue.text: Single sandwich put outside a small car

indicators.note: put outside means the two words go either side of the next piece

parts.note: a single is one run in cricket
a round is a sandwich made from two slices of bread

explanation.surface: A lone snack goes outside with somebody's little car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put outside' places both pieces either side of A. In Britain a round is one whole sandwich, and a runaround is a little car for local trips.
explanation.definitionFit: A little runaround is British slang for a small handy car for local trips.

clue.text: Bout on shore without sun for renegade

indicators.note: in a down clue, on places the first piece above the second

parts.note: a turn is a spell or bout of activity

indicators.note: without means the shore word loses the letter for sun

parts.note: the coast is the shore

explanation.surface: A spell on the beach without any sunshine for a deserter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without sun' removes S from COAST, leaving COAT.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who switches sides or betrays a cause is a traitor.

clue.text: Two notes with old instrument? That's determined

parts.note: re is the second note of the sol-fa scale
so is the fifth note of the sol-fa scale
the lute is an early stringed instrument

explanation.surface: A couple of notes on an ancient instrument show resolve.
explanation.definitionFit: Firm in purpose and unwavering.

clue.text: Woman gets help possibly with no end of pleading

indicators.note: possibly suggests the letters could be arranged another way
with no means the letter taken from the next word is removed
end of picks the last letter of the next word

explanation.surface: A lady receives assistance, perhaps without having to beg.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with no end of pleading' takes the G out of GETS HELP, and 'possibly' rearranges ETSHELP.
explanation.definitionFit: Elspeth is a Scottish female name.

clue.text: Land encompassing river? Certainly!

indicators.note: encompassing means the land word surrounds the next piece

parts.note: to alight is to come down and land

explanation.surface: Touch down by a river? Absolutely!
explanation.walkthrough: 'encompassing' puts R inside ALIGHT.
explanation.definitionFit: An exclamation of agreement or assent, like OK.

clue.text: Excessively fat lout sadly consuming first sign of alcohol

indicators.note: consuming means the rearranged letters swallow the next piece
sadly suggests the words are in a sorry state, so their letters are disordered
first sign of picks the opening letter of the next word

explanation.surface: An overweight yob, sadly drinking, takes things too far.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sadly' makes TOFAULT, and 'consuming' swallows the A picked out by 'first sign of alcohol'.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something to the point of a flaw means overdoing it.

clue.text: A book with recipe put off? It's unexpected

parts.note: R, from the Latin recipe, heads prescriptions

indicators.note: off means the word put is in a bad state, so its letters are muddled

explanation.surface: A cookery book whose recipe has been postponed? That's surprising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' rearranges PUT into UPT. R for recipe is the symbol at the head of a prescription.
explanation.definitionFit: Sudden and without warning.

clue.text: Specify a shop's board, we hear

indicators.note: we hear signals that the words are judged by how they are spoken

parts.note: a sign is the board over a shop front

explanation.surface: Ask for a particular shop's signboard by ear.
explanation.definitionFit: To allot or designate something is to name it.

clue.text: Taxmen with a leading question for me native

parts.note: IR is the Inland Revenue, the old British tax office

indicators.note: leading picks the first letter of the next word

parts.note: the speaker, me, is I

explanation.surface: Tax inspectors with a probing question for me, a local.
explanation.walkthrough: The Inland Revenue was Britain's tax authority before 2005.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone from Baghdad or Basra is a native of that Middle Eastern country.

clue.text: Losing head, Scot in car transported drug

indicators.note: transported means the letters are carried off and put down in a new order
losing head means the first letter is cut from the next word

explanation.surface: A Scotsman in a car, losing his head, is carried away by drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Losing head' trims SCOT to COT, and 'transported' rearranges COT IN CAR.
explanation.definitionFit: An addictive substance that dulls the senses, such as an opiate.

clue.text: Associate happily with some backing song? No late glitch

indicators.note: backing says the hidden letters are read backwards
some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A backing track with no last-minute hitch keeps everyone on good terms.
explanation.walkthrough: Reading 'sonG NO LATE Glitch' backwards gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on friendly terms with someone is the phrasal-verb sense.

clue.text: Powerful publication once ending in library

parts.note: Punch was a British humorous magazine, now defunct

indicators.note: ending in picks the last letter of the next word

explanation.surface: A forceful magazine of old ends up in the library.
explanation.walkthrough: Punch was a satirical British weekly that closed in 2002.
explanation.definitionFit: Forceful and effective, as with a strong drink or a vigorous style.

clue.text: Fast runner and writer

explanation.surface: A sprinter who is also an author.
explanation.definitionFit: Linford Christie was an Olympic champion sprinter; Agatha Christie wrote detective novels.
